title: 1. Easy
question: I have keys but open no locks. I have space but no room. You can enter, but you cannot walk inside me. What am I?
description: A classic riddle where the words "keys," "space," and "enter" point toward a computer object

title: 2. Easy
question: I speak without a mouth and hear without ears. I have no body, but I come alive when sound reaches me. What am I?
description: Identify the phenomenon that repeats a sound
hints: You often hear me in mountains

title: 3. Easy
question: The more you take from me, the bigger I become. What am I?
description: The answer is something that grows when material is removed from it

title: 4. Easy
question: I have a face and two hands, but no arms or legs. What am I?
description: Use the clues about a face and hands to identify the object
hints: I may hang on a wall

title: 5. Easy
question: I get wetter as I dry something else. What am I?
description: Think of an everyday object whose purpose involves drying
hints: You use me after a shower

title: 6. Easy
question: I have one eye but cannot see. What am I?
description: The word "eye" refers to a hole rather than an actual organ

title: 7. Easy

description: Identify the object that decreases in size while producing light

title: 8. Easy
question: I have teeth but cannot bite. What am I?
description: "Teeth" are used metaphorically to describe a common object

title: 9. Easy

description: Identify the natural object associated with darkness and rain

title: 10. Easy

title: 11. Easy
question: I am full of holes, but I can still hold water. What am I?
description: Find the object whose holes are small enough to retain liquid through surface tension
hints: You may find me in a kitchen

title: 12. Easy
question: I have pages but I am not a tree. I contain stories but cannot speak. What am I?
description: The clues point to a common source of written stories

title: 13. Easy
question: I follow you everywhere during the day but disappear when the light is gone. What am I?
description: Identify the dark shape produced by blocking light

title: 14. Easy
question: I have numbers and hands but cannot clap. What am I?
description: Identify the object using the clues "numbers" and "hands."

title: 15. Easy

description: The same word fits several common expressions

title: 16. Easy

description: Think of something that exists only while it remains unspoken
hints: I involve the absence of sound

title: 17. Easy
question: I am always coming but never arrive. What am I?
description: The answer is a concept related to time
hints: When I arrive, I become today

title: 18. Easy
question: I have a thumb and four fingers, but I am not alive. What am I?
description: Identify the object shaped like a hand

title: 19. Easy
question: I can travel around the world while staying in one corner. What am I?
description: The riddle refers to something placed in a corner of an envelope
hints: I am usually stuck to an envelope

title: 20. Easy
question: I am black when clean and white when dirty. What am I?
description: Think of a surface used for writing with chalk

title: 21. Medium
question: I can be written, broken, kept, and given. What am I?
description: Find the word that forms all four common expressions
hints: You can make me to someone

Keeping me means honoring your word

title: 22. Medium
question: I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, and water but no fish. What am I?

title: 39. Medium

title: 40. Medium

title: 49. Hard
question: 19-5-3-18-5-20 uses A=1. What hidden word appears?
description: Decode each number as an alphabet position

title: 50. Hard

description: Extract every third word from the sentence

title: 51. Hard
question: Read the last letters of: "cyber hunt code". What hidden sequence appears?
description: The clue is hidden using word endings

title: 54. Hard

title: 55. Hard

title: 56. Hard
question: A note contains the words "Red Orange Yellow Green Blue." Take their first letters. What hidden word appears?
description: The clue is concealed through the initial letters of color names

title: 57. Hard
question: "SILENT" is written backward. What hidden word appears when you reverse it?
description: Recognize that the clue must be read in reverse order

title: 58. Hard
question: The clue is "LFMMP." Every letter is one position after the intended letter in the alphabet. What word is hidden?
description: Shift each letter backward by one position

title: 59. Hard
question: "Uifsf" was created by shifting every alphabet letter forward by one. What was the original word?

title: 60. Hard
question: A paper says: "Look between the lines." The visible lines are: C A T X Y Z Read only the letters that appear between the first and last letters of each line. What hidden sequence appears?

hints: Ignore the first and last characters
Read the middle letters from top to bottom

title: Q1. The First Search
question: You are given the name of a public organization and asked to find its official website. What should you search for first?

hints: Start with the organization's exact name

title: Q2. Username Hunt
question: A person uses the username tech_raj on one public platform. What can you try searching to find whether the same username exists elsewhere?
description: OSINT often begins by connecting publicly visible usernames

title: Q3. Image Search
question: You receive an image and want to know where it appeared online before. Which type of search is most useful?
description: Identify the technique used to find visually similar or identical images
hints: You don't need to describe the image

title: Q4. Public Information
question: Information that anyone can legally access on the internet is generally called what?
description: This is the foundation of OSINT
hints: It can come from websites, news, maps, etc

title: Q5. Website Date
question: You find two articles about the same event. One was published in 2020 and another in 2024. Which one is generally more recent?
description: OSINT requires checking dates before trusting information

title: Q6. Fake Account Clue
question: An account has thousands of followers but was created yesterday. What should this make you do?
description: Identify a suspicious digital footprint

title: Q7. Location Clue
question: A photograph shows a famous tower. You recognize the tower. What can this information help you determine?
description: Visual clues can reveal a location

title: Q8. Map Investigation
question: You know the name of a restaurant but not where it is. Which online tool would be useful for locating it?
description: Use publicly available geographic information

title: Q9. Username Consistency
question: You find the same unique username on three public websites. What might this suggest?
description: Repeated usernames can be a useful clue
hints: It is a clue, not absolute proof

title: Q10. Source Check
question: Before believing an online claim, what should you check first?
description: Reliable OSINT requires source verification
hints: Don't rely only on the headline

title: Q11. Search Quotes

description: Search operators can make investigations easier
hints: They are commonly used for exact searches

title: Q12. Social Media Clue
question: A public social-media post says someone attended an event on 15 August. What information does this provide?
description: Public posts can provide timeline clues
hints: It gives a point in time
It can help build a timeline

title: Q13. News Verification
question: Two websites report different information about the same event. What should you do?
description: Good investigators compare multiple sources

title: Q14. Domain Clue
question: A website ends with .edu. What type of organization is it commonly associated with?
description: Domain extensions can provide useful context

title: Q15. Photo Detail
question: You are given a street photograph. Which visible clue could help identify the country?
description: Small visual details can reveal location

title: Q16. Metadata
question: Information stored inside a digital file, such as creation date or camera model, is called what?
description: This information can sometimes provide useful investigation clues
hints: It is information about the file
It is not necessarily visible in the picture

title: Q17. Public Records
question: Government websites sometimes publish information that anyone can access. What type of information is this from an OSINT perspective?
description: Public records are legitimate OSINT sources
hints: It comes from an official source

title: Q18. Screenshot Clue
question: A screenshot contains a visible browser address bar. Why can this be useful?
description: Small pieces of visible information can lead to the original source
hints: Look at the top of the browser
It may contain a website address

title: Q19. Search Engine
question: Which tool is commonly used to discover publicly available webpages?
description: Identify a basic OSINT tool

title: Q20. Evidence
question: An investigator finds a claim on social media. Should the claim itself be considered proof?
description: OSINT requires distinguishing claims from verified evidence

title: Q21. Exact Username
question: You are investigating the username bluefox27. Searching "bluefox27" gives results on several websites. What is the next logical step?
description: Finding the same username is only the beginning
hints: Don't assume all accounts belong to one person

title: Q22. Profile Picture
question: A public account uses a distinctive profile picture. What technique can help determine whether the picture appears elsewhere?
description: Images can reveal connections to other public pages

title: Q23. Timeline

description: Investigators often organize clues according to time

title: Q24. Conflicting Dates
question: A website says an event happened on Monday, but the published date was Tuesday. What should you do?
description: Inconsistencies should be investigated rather than ignored
hints: Don't immediately assume either source is correct

title: Q25. Same Photo
question: You find the same photograph on two websites, but one website claims it was taken in India and the other claims it was taken in France. What should you check?
description: Context around an image can be misleading

title: Q26. Map Clue
question: A photo shows a road sign saying NH 44. Which type of information can this clue provide?
description: Road numbers can narrow down locations

title: Q27. Domain Investigation
question: You find a suspicious website claiming to belong to a company. The company's official website uses a different domain. What should you compare?
description: Domain comparison can expose misleading websites
hints: Look for extra words or characters

title: Q28. Archived Page

description: Websites can sometimes be viewed through historical archives
hints: One famous service is the Wayback Machine

title: Q29. Image Timestamp
question: A photo's metadata says it was created in 2022, but someone claims it was taken in 2025. What should you do?
description: Metadata can be useful but should not automatically be treated as absolute proof

title: Q30. Multiple Sources
question: One unknown blog makes a claim. Five independent reputable news organizations report the same event. Which has stronger support?
description: Independent sources can increase confidence

title: Q31. Search Operator
question: You want search results only from example.com. Which search technique is useful?
description: Search operators can narrow results

title: Q32. Public Username + Bio
question: A username is found on two platforms. One profile contains the same public website link as the other. Does this provide stronger evidence of a connection?
description: Multiple matching clues are more useful than one

title: Q33. Location from Background
question: A photograph has no location tag, but a shop sign in the background contains a city name. Can the sign help identify the location?
description: Text in images can be valuable evidence

title: Q34. Fake News
question: An old photograph is reposted with a new event description. What should you investigate?
description: Images can be reused with incorrect context

title: Q35. Public Email Clue
question: A company employee publicly lists their professional email on a company webpage. Is this considered publicly available information?
description: OSINT focuses on information legitimately available to the public
hints: It is on an official page

title: Q36. Review Investigation
question: A restaurant has hundreds of reviews, but almost all were posted within two days. What should you investigate?
description: Unusual patterns can indicate unreliable information
hints: Think whether the activity looks natural

title: Q37. Photo + Map
question: You identify a landmark in a photo. What can you use next to determine nearby streets?
description: OSINT often combines multiple public sources

title: Q38. Source Reliability
question: Which is generally more reliable for an official government announcement: an anonymous social-media account or the government's official website?
description: Source authority matters

title: Q39. Search Result Comparison
question: Search A gives 100 results while Search B gives 5 highly relevant results. Which search is potentially more useful for investigation?
description: More results do not necessarily mean better results

title: Q40. Investigator's Rule
question: You have one strong clue and three weak clues pointing toward the same conclusion. Should you immediately declare the conclusion proven?
description: OSINT requires careful confidence assessment

title: Q41. Username + Location
question: You find the same unique username on three public platforms. Platform A mentions a city, Platform B mentions a university, and Platform C shows a public event photo. What should you do before connecting all three accounts?
description: OSINT investigations should avoid assumptions based on a single matching identifier
hints: Check whether the dates make sense

title: Q42. The Old Photograph
question: A viral post claims a photograph was taken yesterday. Reverse image searching shows the same photograph online five years ago. What is the strongest conclusion?
description: The photograph may be genuine but its current context may be false

title: Q43. Three Sources
question: Website A copies Website B, and Website B copied an anonymous post. Can A and B be considered two independent confirmations?
description: Source independence is important
hints: Two copies aren't two independent sources

title: Q44. Digital Footprint
question: A person publicly uses the same unique nickname, avatar, and personal website across several platforms. What is being created by these repeated clues?
description: Repeated public information forms a recognizable online presence

title: Q45. Metadata Conflict
question: An image's metadata says it was taken in Delhi, but visible signs clearly indicate another country. Which should you trust automatically?
description: Different evidence sources can conflict
hints: Metadata can be altered or lost
Visual evidence can also be misinterpreted

title: Q46. Search Narrowing
question: You search for Apple and receive millions of results. You then search Apple "Bangalore" "2025". Why did the second search produce more focused results?
description: Adding specific terms reduces irrelevant results

title: Q47. Hidden Context
question: A screenshot shows a message but hides the website name. The browser tab title is visible and contains a unique phrase. What could you do with the phrase?
description: Small pieces of visible information can become search clues

title: Q48. Location Puzzle
question: A photo contains: - a red-and-white road sign, - a left-driving road, - a shop displaying prices in ₹. Which country is the strongest initial possibility?
description: Multiple clues can be combined to narrow a location

title: Q49. Event Verification
question: A poster says an event happened on 12 March. A public video from the event is uploaded on 13 March, and an official event page lists 12 March. How many independent clues support the date?
description: Combine evidence from different sources
hints: Count the video upload date carefully
Upload date isn't necessarily event date

title: Q50. Fake Profile Detection
question: A profile claims to have worked at a company since 2018, but the company's public employee announcement shows the person joined in 2023. What should you investigate?
description: Conflicting public timelines can reveal inaccurate claims
hints: Don't immediately label the person fraudulent

title: Q51. Source Chain
question: You discover that five websites all use exactly the same unusual sentence when reporting an event. What should you investigate?
description: Similar wording can indicate that multiple websites are relying on one original source

title: Q52. Map + Photograph

description: Combining visual and geographic clues can increase confidence

title: Q53. Account Attribution

description: A common identifier does not automatically establish identity

title: Q54. Old Website
question: A company's current website no longer lists a product. You want to know whether the company previously offered it. What can you investigate?
description: Historical webpages may preserve information that is no longer visible

title: Q55. Geolocation
question: You have a street photograph with no obvious landmark. You notice language, road markings, architecture, vehicle plates, and shop names. What OSINT task are you performing?
description: Multiple visual clues are used to determine where an image was taken
hints: The common OSINT term begins with "Geo."

title: Q56. Information Reliability
question: Source A is an anonymous post. Source B is a dated official government document. Source C is a blog quoting Source A. Which is generally the strongest primary source?
description: Source type and proximity to the original information matter

title: Q57. Contradictory Evidence
question: Four clues suggest Location X, but one highly reliable official source says Location Y. What should an investigator do?
description: OSINT is not simply about counting clues

title: Q58. Search Evolution
question: Your first search gives irrelevant results. You add a location, date, and exact phrase and get useful results. What OSINT skill are you demonstrating?
description: Effective investigators refine their searches based on results

title: Q59. Final Verification
question: You believe you have identified the location of a photograph. What is the best final step before reporting your conclusion?
description: A good investigation verifies the conclusion using independent evidence
hints: Don't stop after the first match

title: Q60. The OSINT Principle
question: Which is better OSINT practice? A. Believe the first result B. Assume matching usernames are the same person C. Collect, compare, and verify public information D. Trust viral posts
description: This question tests the fundamental mindset behind OSINT

title: 30. Pair Sum

title: 31. Position Product

title: 32. Difference Code

title: 33. Middle Letter

title: 35. Reverse Number

description: Reverse the sequence of numbers

title: 36. Letter-Number Conversion

title: 37. Shift by Word Length

title: 38. Reverse and Shift

title: 39. Odd-Even Code

title: 40. Alphabet Mirror

title: 41. Double Shift

title: 47. Sum of All Letters

title: 1. Fake Login Page
question: A person creates a fake Instagram login page and sends you the link to steal your password. What is this called?
description: The attacker tricks a user into believing a fake website is genuine

title: 2. Password Guessing
question: Someone keeps trying different passwords until they successfully log into an account. What is this attack called?
description: The attacker repeatedly guesses passwords
hints: Think about using force instead of intelligence

title: 3. Weak Password
question: A user sets their password as 123456. What security problem does this represent?
description: Simple passwords are much easier for attackers to guess

title: 4. Website Script
question: An attacker puts harmful JavaScript into a website's comment box, and visitors see it when they open the page. What vulnerability is this?
description: The website allows unwanted scripts to run in a user's browser
hints: Its common abbreviation has three letters

title: 5. SQL Database
question: A website directly places what a user types into a database query without checking it properly. What vulnerability can result?
description: Attackers may manipulate the database query through specially crafted input

title: 6. Fake Email
question: You receive an email pretending to be from your bank asking you to click a suspicious link and enter your password. What is this?
description: The attacker impersonates a trusted organization
hints: It is a type of social engineering

title: 7. Public Password
question: A developer accidentally uploads a file containing the website's database password to a public repository. What security problem has occurred?
description: A secret has been accidentally exposed to others
hints: Think about sensitive information becoming visible

title: 8. Unlocked Account
question: You leave your account logged in on a public computer. Someone else opens it and uses it. What security problem allowed this?
description: An active login session was left accessible to another person
hints: The next person didn't need your password

title: 9. Unsafe Website
question: Which protocol should you look for when entering a password or card details on a website?
description: It encrypts communication between your browser and the website
hints: Look at the beginning of the web address
It has a padlock in most browsers

title: 10. Website Permission
question: A normal user somehow opens an admin-only page. What type of security problem is this?
description: The website failed to properly check whether the user was allowed to access the page

title: 11. Dangerous Download
question: A website tricks you into downloading a harmful program disguised as a useful file. What is the file commonly called?
description: Attackers may disguise malicious software as legitimate downloads
hints: It pretends to be something useful

title: 12. Website Disguise
question: A website uses a name and design very similar to a popular shopping website to fool customers. What is this?
description: The attacker creates a deceptive copy of a legitimate website
hints: The goal is to fool visitors
It is often connected to phishing

title: 13. Too Many Requests
question: A user sends thousands of requests to a website in a short time, slowing it down. What type of attack is this?
description: Excessive traffic can make a website slow or unavailable
hints: The website becomes difficult to access

title: 14. Many Computers
question: What is an attack called when many computers are used together to overwhelm a website?
description: Multiple devices generate a large amount of traffic against a target
hints: The first letter stands for Distributed

title: 15. Secret Information
question: A website displays a user's credit-card number openly on their profile. What security issue is this?
description: Sensitive information should not be unnecessarily visible
hints: The information is visible when it shouldn't be

title: 16. Old Software
question: A website continues using an old version of software even though a security update is available. What is the main problem?
description: Older software may contain vulnerabilities that have already been fixed

title: 17. Remember Me
question: A website uses a small piece of information stored in your browser to remember that you are logged in. What is it?
description: Websites commonly use this mechanism for sessions and preferences
hints: You can clear it from browser settings

title: 18. Login Verification
question: What security feature asks for a password AND a code sent to your phone?
description: Using two different verification steps provides stronger account protection

title: 19. Human Trick
question: An attacker calls an employee pretending to be an IT technician and asks for their password. What type of attack is this?
description: Instead of attacking software, the attacker manipulates a person
hints: No hacking tool is necessarily required

title: 20. Security Lock
question: What symbol in a browser usually indicates that the connection to a website is encrypted?
description: Browsers commonly display a lock icon for secure HTTPS connections
hints: It looks like a small locked object

title: 21. Changing the ID
question: You open /profile/101, change the number to /profile/102, and suddenly see another person's profile. What vulnerability might this indicate?
description: The website may not be checking whether you are actually allowed to access that person's data

title: 22. Unlimited Attempts
question: A login page allows you to try 10,000 passwords without blocking or slowing you down. What security control is missing?
description: Websites should restrict excessive login attempts
hints: It controls how frequently something can happen

title: 23. The Secret URL
question: An admin page is not linked anywhere on the website, but anyone can access it if they know its URL. Is hiding the URL enough security?
description: Simply hiding a page does not replace proper access control
hints: A secret URL isn't a permission system
Anyone with the URL can enter

title: 24. Login Link
question: A password-reset link contains a predictable number such as reset?id=12345. Why can this be dangerous?
description: Predictable reset information can make account recovery mechanisms easier to abuse
hints: Reset links should be difficult to guess
Attackers should not be able to predict another user's link

title: 25. Comment Box
question: A website displays exactly what users type into a comment box without safely handling special characters. Which vulnerability could result?
description: User input that becomes executable content can affect other visitors
hints: This is a common web vulnerability

title: 26. Fake Discount
question: An online store allows a user to apply the same discount coupon 100 times because the server never checks the limit. What kind of vulnerability is this?
description: The application fails to enforce its intended business rules
hints: The problem is with the business rule
Think about "how the system is supposed to work."

title: 27. Public File
question: A website accidentally makes its database backup downloadable through a public URL. What security problem is this?
description: Sensitive internal files should not be publicly accessible
hints: Anyone with the link can access it

title: 28. Trusted Request
question: You are logged into your bank. You visit another website, and that website secretly causes your browser to send a request to your bank. What attack is this?
description: The malicious website attempts to make your authenticated browser perform an unwanted action
hints: It is commonly shortened to four letters

title: 29. Password Reuse
question: A password leaked from one website is successfully used to log into another website. What attack takes advantage of this?
description: Attackers exploit users reusing the same credentials across different services
hints: Think about using leaked credentials again

title: 30. File Upload
question: A website allows users to upload profile pictures but accepts any type of file. Why can this be dangerous?
description: Unrestricted uploads can allow users to place unexpected or harmful files on the server
hints: The user can upload something else

title: 31. Error Message
question: A website error reveals its database name, server location, and programming language. What security problem is this?
description: Detailed error messages can reveal information useful to attackers
hints: The website is revealing too much
Developers may find the information useful

title: 32. Open Redirect
question: A website has a "Continue" button that sends users to any URL supplied in the address bar. What vulnerability could this create?
description: Attackers can use trusted domains to redirect victims to malicious websites
hints: The website isn't the final destination
The destination is controlled by the URL

title: 33. Website Trust
question: A website trusts everything a user enters because it assumes "users won't enter anything harmful." What security principle is being violated?
description: User input should always be treated carefully rather than automatically trusted

title: 34. Database Password
question: A developer stores the database password directly inside publicly visible JavaScript code. What has been exposed?
description: Secrets should not be placed where users can easily retrieve them
hints: JavaScript runs in the user's browser

title: 35. Admin Privileges
question: A normal employee changes "role=user" to "role=admin" in a request and becomes an administrator. What security control failed?
description: The server should determine and enforce the user's privileges rather than trusting client-controlled values
hints: The client changed its own role

title: 36. Secure Password Storage
question: A website stores everyone's passwords as plain readable text in its database. What is the biggest security problem?
description: Anyone obtaining the database could immediately read users' passwords

title: 37. Same Password
question: Why is using the same password on every website dangerous?
description: A breach at one service can give attackers credentials that work elsewhere
hints: One leak can affect many accounts
Different sites should have different passwords

title: 38. No Logout
question: A website's session remains active even after the user clicks "Logout." What security area should be investigated?
description: Logout should invalidate the user's active session appropriately

title: 39. Unnecessary Information
question: A website tells you "Username exists, but password is wrong" instead of giving the same message for both cases. What information can this reveal?
description: Different responses can help attackers discover valid accounts
hints: The attacker learns something without logging in
It is a type of information leakage

title: 40. Automatic Updates
question: A website uses a third-party library that has a known security flaw but the developer never updates it. What is the main weakness?
description: Vulnerable dependencies can introduce security problems into otherwise well-written applications
hints: The problem comes from another package

title: 41. The Free Product
question: An online store lets users change the product price in their browser from ₹5,000 to ₹5 before submitting the order. The server accepts ₹5. What failed?
description: The server trusted a value controlled by the user instead of calculating the price itself
hints: The browser should not decide the final price
The server should verify important values

title: 42. The Hidden Admin
question: A normal user changes /user/dashboard to /admin/dashboard and gains access. What security problem is demonstrated?
description: The server is not properly checking whether the logged-in user has administrative privileges
hints: Authentication isn't the same as permission

title: 43. The Unlimited Coupon
question: A coupon should work once per customer, but refreshing the page allows it to be applied repeatedly. What type of vulnerability is this?
description: The application failed to enforce a business restriction

title: 44. The Changed Account
question: A website uses /account?id=500. Changing 500 to 501 displays another user's private account. What is the vulnerability?
description: The application uses a user-controlled identifier without correctly checking ownership
hints: You may have seen this abbreviation before

title: 45. The Helpful Error
question: A login page responds differently when the username exists versus when it doesn't. What can an attacker perform using this difference?
description: Response differences can reveal which usernames are registered
hints: The attacker doesn't need the password

title: 46. The Fake Reset
question: A password-reset token is always username123. Why is this dangerous?
description: A reset token should be difficult to predict. Predictable tokens can allow unauthorized password resets

title: 47. The Open Door API
question: An API returns private customer information whenever someone provides a customer ID, without checking who is making the request. What is missing?
description: The API authenticates or processes requests but fails to enforce who is allowed to access the requested data
hints: It doesn't check the user's permission

title: 48. The Trusted Browser
question: A website accepts a request simply because it comes from a logged-in user's browser, even though another website caused the request. What vulnerability could occur?
description: The server incorrectly assumes that a request from an authenticated browser was intentionally made by the user

title: 49. The Comment Attack
question: A user posts <script> in a comment and the code runs whenever someone views the comment. What vulnerability is this?
description: User-controlled content is being interpreted as executable browser code

title: 50. The Database Trick
question: A login form builds a database query directly using the username typed by the user. What vulnerability should the developer worry about?
description: Untrusted input can alter the intended database query if it is not safely handled

title: 51. The Server's Request
question: A website asks users for a URL and then fetches that URL from its own server. Why could this become dangerous?
description: If the server doesn't restrict destinations, an attacker may cause it to request resources the attacker shouldn't be able to reach

title: 52. The Fake Destination
question: A trusted website redirects users to any website specified by a URL parameter. Why could attackers abuse this?
description: Attackers may send victims a trusted-looking link that ultimately leads to a malicious website
hints: The first website may be legitimate
The final website is controlled by the attacker

title: 53. The Unlimited Login
question: An attacker can make thousands of login attempts per second because the website has no restriction on request frequency. What protection is missing?
description: Limiting repeated requests can make automated attacks much harder
hints: It is called limiting the request rate

title: 54. The Password Database
question: A hacker steals a database containing passwords stored in a form that can be read immediately. What protection should have been used?
description: Passwords should be stored using secure one-way password hashing rather than readable text
hints: Modern applications use password hashing algorithms

title: 55. The Public Backup
question: A developer accidentally uploads database_backup.zip to the website's public folder. What vulnerability could this create?
description: Backup files may contain credentials, customer information, or other sensitive data
hints: Backups can contain lots of information

title: 56. The Dangerous Upload
question: A profile-picture page accepts .jpg, .png, .exe, and .html files without checking them. What security weakness does this demonstrate?
description: The application does not properly restrict uploads to the intended file types

title: 57. The Old Library
question: A website uses an outdated library with a publicly known security flaw. What should the developer do first?
description: Known vulnerabilities should be addressed by updating or replacing affected dependencies

title: 58. The Password in URL
question: A website sends a user's password as part of the URL, such as example.com/login?password=12345. Why is this unsafe?
description: URLs can appear in browser history, logs, analytics systems, and other places

title: 59. The Admin Cookie
question: A website stores an administrator's session information in a cookie that can be accessed by JavaScript. Why could this be dangerous if XSS exists?
description: If malicious JavaScript executes in the browser, it may be able to access sensitive session information when cookie protections are missing
hints: Think about protecting cookies from JavaScript

title: 60. The Biggest Clue
question: A website accepts user input, trusts it completely, and directly uses it in HTML, database queries, commands, and file paths. What general security principle should developers follow?
description: User-controlled data should be treated as untrusted and appropriately checked before being used
